blocks.text: Aim
Recognise the geometry of a shielded metal arc welded corner joint. The drawing is a conceptual view, without welding parameters.
Tools Required
Steel rule; marking tool; square; clamps; welding equipment and instructor-specified PPE.
Materials Required
Two metal plates and a compatible electrode selected for the approved exercise.
Working Principle
An electric arc supplies local heat to join the prepared plate edges. The coated electrode also contributes filler and protection around the weld zone.
Diagram
Sequence of Operation
1. Prepare and inspect the work area and equipment under supervision.
2. Check the plate edges and mark the intended joint position.
3. Hold the plates in the required corner arrangement and check alignment.
4. Secure the assembly using the instructor-approved tacking and joining method.
5. After cooling, inspect the joint visually and compare its geometry with the approved drawing.
Observation and Inference

rows: The two faces meet at the intended corner.
The bead follows the meeting edge; appearance alone does not prove strength.
Distortion and visible discontinuities are points for inspection.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What does SMAW stand for?
Answer: Shielded Metal Arc Welding.
2. What does the highlighted line identify?
Answer: The meeting edge where the two plates are joined; it does not specify a weld size or operating setting.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why is alignment checked before joining?
Answer: Joining can lock the pieces in place, making an initial positioning error harder to correct.
2. Why should hot work be supervised?
Answer: Arc radiation, hot metal, fumes and electrical equipment require appropriate controls and training.
Results

Expected learning outcome: Recognise the geometry of a shielded metal arc welded corner joint. The drawing is a conceptual view, without welding parameters. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.
Aim
Identify the structural steps, lighting positions and separate low-voltage circuit in a staircase assembly.
Tools Required
Rule; square; marking and holding tools; approved joining equipment; low-voltage test equipment.
Materials Required
Stair components; base; suitable light units; switch; insulated conductors; rated low-voltage supply.
Working Principle
The staircase is the supporting structure. A separate electrical circuit allows a switch to control light units mounted at selected locations.
Diagram

blocks.label: Staircase Welding and Lighting Assembly — conceptual diagram

blocks.text: Sequence of Operation
1. Identify all structural parts from the approved drawing.
2. Check the stair positions and assemble the structure using the specified joining method.
3. Inspect the cooled structure and finish sharp edges using the approved procedure.
4. With power disconnected, arrange the rated low-voltage lights, switch and conductors.
5. Have the wiring inspected before energising; check the switch and observe each light.
Observation and Inference

rows: Opening the circuit removes the intended light supply.
Each intended lighting position can be inspected individually.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. Why show the lighting circuit separately?
Answer: It makes the electrical connections easier to distinguish from the staircase structure.
2. Is the circuit a mains-wiring diagram?
Answer: No. It is a conceptual battery-powered light circuit and does not specify a rated practical installation.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why separate mechanical assembly from electrical testing?
Answer: It helps isolate structural issues from circuit issues and avoids working on energised connections.
2. Why check insulation?
Answer: Exposed or damaged conductors may create unintended contact paths.
Results

Expected learning outcome: Identify the structural steps, lighting positions and separate low-voltage circuit in a staircase assembly. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.

blocks.text: Aim
Identify a solar panel, controller, storage battery and load in a conceptual energy system.
Tools Required
Rule; mounting tools; suitable multimeter; instructor-approved wiring tools.
Materials Required
Solar panel; compatible controller; suitable battery where specified; mounting frame; rated load.
Working Principle
A photovoltaic panel converts light into electrical energy. A compatible controller manages the intended electrical interface; a battery can store energy when the selected system includes storage.
Diagram

blocks.label: Solar Based Power Generation System — conceptual diagram

blocks.text: Sequence of Operation
1. Identify the panel, support, controller, storage and load used in the approved system.
2. Check mounting locations and ratings with the instructor.
3. Assemble the support and inspect the panel mounting.
4. Connect the system only according to the approved wiring diagram and inspection procedure.
5. Compare the indicated electrical behaviour under the specified illumination conditions.
Observation and Inference

rows: Panel output may change when illumination changes.
Battery and controller behaviour depends on their specifications.
A connected load uses delivered electrical power.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What is the role of the panel?
Answer: It converts incident light into electrical energy.
2. What is the role of the battery in this example?
Answer: It stores energy for later use. The diagram does not specify battery chemistry, charging settings or component ratings.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why are component ratings important?
Answer: Voltage, current and charging compatibility affect whether the components can operate together.
2. Does a solar panel always deliver its nameplate power?
Answer: No. Actual output depends on conditions including illumination, temperature and load.
Results

Expected learning outcome: Identify a solar panel, controller, storage battery and load in a conceptual energy system. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.

blocks.text: Aim
Understand how complementary recesses permit two wooden strips to cross.
Tools Required
Rule; try square; marking gauge; saw; chisel; mallet; holding tools.
Materials Required
Two suitable wooden members with dimensions specified in the exercise drawing.
Working Principle
Complementary recesses let two crossing members share the overlap region. Accurate marking and controlled material removal determine how well the surfaces meet.
Diagram
Sequence of Operation
1. Examine the two members and identify reference faces.
2. Transfer the overlap position from the approved drawing using the reference faces.
3. Mark and verify the material-removal limits before cutting.
4. Form the recesses using the demonstrated woodworking method.
5. Bring the members together and inspect alignment and contact without forcing the joint.
Observation and Inference

rows: Consistent reference faces help transfer matching marks.
The overlapping surfaces can be examined for uneven seating.
The assembled members can be compared with the required orientation.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. Why show an exploded view?
Answer: It exposes the recesses that become hidden when the members overlap.
2. Does the sketch specify the notch depth?
Answer: No. A dimensioned drawing is needed before constructing a physical joint.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why identify a reference face?
Answer: It gives a consistent origin for marking and checking dimensions.
2. Why avoid forcing the members together?
Answer: Force may hide a size error or damage the material instead of correcting the fit.
Results
Expected learning outcome: Understand how complementary recesses permit two wooden strips to cross. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.
Aim
Distinguish the major wooden components and the pivot joints in a robot-shaped model.
Tools Required
Rule; square; marking tools; supervised cutting and drilling equipment; finishing tools.
Materials Required
Wooden head, body and limb pieces; approved pins or fasteners; adhesive where specified.
Working Principle
A robot-shaped model combines distinct members into a body assembly. Depending on the design, joint connections may be fixed or permit rotation.
Diagram
Sequence of Operation
1. Identify the head, body and limb components in the approved drawing.
2. Mark the piece outlines and joint positions using consistent references.
3. Prepare the pieces with the supervised cutting and drilling procedure.
4. Finish rough edges and assemble the specified connections.
5. Check the resulting shape and any intended articulation.
Observation and Inference

rows: Head, body and limbs remain distinguishable.
Fixed connections and movable pivots serve different purposes.
Articulation depends on the selected joint design.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What do the circles represent?
Answer: Simplified pivot connections between the model’s components.
2. Does the model need to be powered?
Answer: A wooden model can be static or articulated. The actual experiment requirements depend on the faculty-approved design.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why finish edges before final assembly?
Answer: Finishing is often easier while the separate faces are accessible.
2. Why should pivot holes align?
Answer: Misaligned holes can interfere with a pin or prevent the intended movement.
Results

Expected learning outcome: Distinguish the major wooden components and the pivot joints in a robot-shaped model. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.
Aim
Identify the motor-driven pivot, arm links and end attachment of a simplified robotic arm.
Tools Required
Rule; assembly tools; suitable electrical test equipment; instructor-approved control tools.
Materials Required
Base; arm links; joint connections; motor or actuator; compatible driver and supply; end attachment.
Working Principle
A motor-driven joint changes the relative orientation of connected links. The power supply, driver, transmission and control method must match the selected actuator and mechanism.
Diagram

blocks.label: Motorized Robotic Arm Activation — conceptual diagram

blocks.text: Sequence of Operation
1. Identify the base, links, joint connections and actuator in the approved design.
2. Assemble the mechanical structure and check clearance with power disconnected.
3. Install the actuator using the specified mounting and coupling.
4. Have the supply and control connections checked against the approved circuit.
5. Test only the allowed motion range under supervision and observe interference or binding.
Observation and Inference

rows: The joint defines where relative rotation occurs.
Links need room for the intended movement.
Command and motion depend on the particular actuator and controller.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What is the motor’s role?
Answer: To provide rotational motion at a driven joint through a suitable connection.
2. Is a motor alone a complete arm control system?
Answer: No. Power, mechanical coupling, control and suitable limits depend on the actual implementation.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why test for binding before powering the mechanism?
Answer: A jammed joint can prevent motion and place excessive demand on the actuator.
2. Does adding a motor make an arm autonomous?
Answer: No. Autonomous behaviour additionally needs an appropriate control system and information about the task.
Results

Expected learning outcome: Identify the motor-driven pivot, arm links and end attachment of a simplified robotic arm. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.

blocks.text: Aim
Identify the base, four walls and fold lines of a conceptual rectangular tray.
Tools Required
Rule; square; scriber; appropriate cutting and forming tools; edge-finishing tools.
Materials Required
Suitable sheet material and joining materials, if required by the approved tray design.
Working Principle
A flat layout identifies the base and wall regions. Forming changes the wall orientations; a practical layout must account for thickness, bend behaviour and corner construction.
Diagram
Sequence of Operation
1. Identify the base, wall heights and corner treatment from the dimensioned drawing.
2. Prepare the approved layout including the specified bend information.
3. Mark and verify cut and bend locations before material removal.
4. Cut, finish edges and form the walls using the demonstrated method.
5. Complete the required corner connections and inspect the tray geometry.
Observation and Inference

rows: The central region corresponds to the base.
Walls surround the base to create an open volume.
Corner construction depends on the specified design.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. Which region becomes the tray base?
Answer: The central rectangle in the unfolded layout.
2. Why can’t this flat net be used as a cutting template?
Answer: It has no dimensions, material thickness, bend allowance or joining details.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why is edge finishing necessary?
Answer: Cut sheet edges can be sharp and can interfere with assembly or handling.
2. What is missing from a purely visual net?
Answer: It does not establish working dimensions, thickness compensation or the intended corner connection.
Results
Expected learning outcome: Identify the base, four walls and fold lines of a conceptual rectangular tray. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.
Aim
Study the chassis, wheels, mast and fork carriage before assembly.
Tools Required
Measuring and marking tools; supervised cutting and drilling tools; assembly tools.
Materials Required
Chassis; mast supports; wheels and axles; fork carriage; motor mount; approved fasteners.
Working Principle
Fabrication prepares the separate structural components and their interfaces so the forklift model can subsequently be assembled and operated as designed.
Diagram

blocks.label: Mini Motorized Forklift Fabrication — conceptual diagram

blocks.text: Sequence of Operation
1. Identify separate chassis, support and carriage pieces from the approved part drawings.
2. Mark outlines, hole locations and interfaces on the selected materials.
3. Check the marks before supervised cutting, drilling and edge finishing.
4. Compare the prepared parts with the drawing and each other.
5. Trial-assemble the structural interfaces before fitting the powered mechanisms.
Observation and Inference

rows: Each prepared part has a defined place in the assembly.
Hole positions and contact faces affect assembly alignment.
A trial fit can reveal interference before final fastening.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What is the mast?
Answer: The upright structure associated with guiding the lifting carriage.
2. Why use a separated component view?
Answer: It helps identify the parts and their relationships before studying the complete assembly.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why distinguish fabrication from final operation?
Answer: A correctly made part still has to be integrated with the rest of the assembly and its drive system.
2. Why inspect hole positions?
Answer: Incorrect positions may prevent parts from aligning or fastening as intended.
Results
Expected learning outcome: Study the chassis, wheels, mast and fork carriage before assembly. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.

blocks.text: Aim
Identify how the carriage is guided by the mast in the assembled model.
Tools Required
Assembly tools; measuring tools; suitable test equipment; instructor-specified safety equipment.
Materials Required
Fabricated chassis; wheels and axles; mast; fork carriage; selected drive and lift components; compatible supply.
Working Principle
The mast guides the carriage while the fork attachment supports an intended load. Propulsion and lifting may use separate mechanisms depending on the approved model.
Diagram
Sequence of Operation
1. Identify the fabricated chassis, mast, carriage and selected drive components.
2. Assemble the chassis, wheels and mast according to the approved arrangement.
3. Install the carriage guides and check free movement with power disconnected.
4. Fit the specified motor, transmission and electrical connections under supervision.
5. Test unloaded movement before any instructor-approved loading exercise.
Observation and Inference

rows: Support geometry and load position affect stability.
Guides constrain the intended carriage path.
Wheel movement and lifting are distinct functions.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What supports the item being lifted?
Answer: The forks attached to the carriage in this conceptual model.
2. Does this sketch establish a safe load?
Answer: No. Load capacity depends on the actual design, materials, stability and testing.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why begin with an unloaded check?
Answer: It helps identify alignment and motion problems before introducing an added load.
2. Can a model’s safe load be read from a sketch?
Answer: No. It requires a suitable design assessment and the approved testing method.
Results
Expected learning outcome: Identify how the carriage is guided by the mast in the assembled model. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.
Aim
Identify a stepped projection and its complementary recess.
Tools Required
Steel rule; square; scriber; bench vice; appropriate saw and files; approved measuring equipment.
Materials Required
Two workpieces with dimensions, material and fitting allowance specified in the drawing.
Working Principle
The stepped projection on one piece corresponds to the recess on the other. Material removal and dimensional checking establish the intended clearance and contact.
Diagram
Sequence of Operation
1. Choose the reference edges and examine the approved dimensions.
2. Mark both stepped profiles and verify the relationships between them.
3. Remove bulk material using the demonstrated supervised method.
4. Approach the specified size progressively with suitable filing and inspection.
5. Compare the pieces and check the fit without forcing them together.
Observation and Inference

rows: Projection and recess have complementary stepped outlines.
Actual fit depends on measured size and specified allowance.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What makes the profiles complementary?
Answer: The stepped projection on one piece corresponds to the recess on the other.
2. Does a matching sketch guarantee a fit?
Answer: No. Actual dimensions, tolerances and inspection determine whether real parts fit.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why remove material progressively near the final size?
Answer: Excess removal cannot be undone by further filing.
2. Why should a fit be checked with measurements?
Answer: Visual similarity does not establish the required dimensions or clearance.
Results
Expected learning outcome: Identify a stepped projection and its complementary recess. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.

title: Scissor Lift Mechanism Fabrication and Assembly

blocks.text: Aim
Explain how crossed links and pivot connections form a scissor lift arrangement.
Tools Required
Rule; marking tools; supervised cutting and drilling tools; assembly tools.
Materials Required
Base; platform; crossed links; pivots; guides or sliding connections; approved actuation components.
Working Principle
Crossed links connected at pivots change platform height as the mechanism changes configuration. Guides or sliding connections accommodate the required relative movement.
Diagram

blocks.label: Scissor Lift Mechanism Fabrication and Assembly — conceptual diagram

blocks.text: Sequence of Operation
1. Identify the base, platform, links, pivots and guides in the approved drawing.
2. Prepare and inspect the link interfaces and joint locations.
3. Assemble the linkage in the specified order with power or loading removed.
4. Check the permitted movement and inspect for binding or interference.
5. Have the completed assembly inspected before any approved actuation or loading test.
Observation and Inference

rows: The crossed members transfer movement through the linkage.
Pivots permit relative rotation at the defined joints.
Travel depends on the actual geometry and constraints.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What connects the two crossed links?
Answer: A pivot at their crossing point in the simplified drawing.
2. Does the diagram establish safe lifting capacity?
Answer: No. It illustrates component relationships, not structural capacity or certified operation.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why can some end connections need to slide?
Answer: Changing link angles can change the horizontal separation required at the endpoints.
2. Why keep hands away from moving joints?
Answer: Moving links and pivots can create trapping and pinch locations.
Results

Expected learning outcome: Explain how crossed links and pivot connections form a scissor lift arrangement. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.

title: Fabrication and Assembly of a DC Motor-Driven Pulley Mechanism for Energy Conversion

blocks.text: Aim
Identify a driving motor, belt, driven pulley and generator in a conceptual energy-conversion arrangement.
Tools Required
Rule; alignment tools; assembly tools; suitable electrical measuring equipment.
Materials Required
Driving DC motor; pulleys and belt; driven generator or motor used as specified; base and supports; compatible supply and load.
Working Principle

The driving motor converts electrical energy into shaft motion. A belt transmits rotation to a driven shaft, and a suitable generator converts part of the mechanical input into electrical output. Losses occur at every stage.
Diagram

blocks.label: Fabrication and Assembly of a DC Motor-Driven Pulley Mechanism for Energy Conversion — conceptual diagram

blocks.text: Sequence of Operation
1. Identify the motor, shafts, pulleys, belt, supports and output device in the approved arrangement.
2. Mount the supports and check the specified shaft and pulley alignment.
3. Install and inspect the belt using the approved tension and guarding method.
4. Have all supply and output connections checked before operation.
5. Run the permitted test under supervision and compare input, rotation and output observations.
Observation and Inference

rows: The driving motor receives electrical power.
The belt carries mechanical motion between pulleys.
The output device can supply a compatible load; losses prevent equal input and output power.

blocks.text: These are explanatory relationships, not measured observations or claims that the physical experiment was performed.
Questions and Answers
Pre Lab Questions
1. What does the belt transmit?
Answer: Mechanical rotation between the driving and driven pulley shafts.
2. Is the final electrical output equal to the electrical input?
Answer: No. Motor, transmission and generator losses mean the arrangement is not a source of free energy.
Post Lab Questions
1. Why check pulley alignment?
Answer: Misalignment can impair belt tracking and increase unwanted wear or losses.
2. Why does this system not create free energy?
Answer: Every stage has losses, so energy delivered to the final load is less than the energy supplied to the system.
Results

Expected learning outcome: Identify a driving motor, belt, driven pulley and generator in a conceptual energy-conversion arrangement. This describes the purpose of the exercise and does not certify a completed practical result.
